title: States of Matter & Particle Model
description: Solids, liquids, gases, changes of state, the particle model, diffusion, gas pressure, and heating/cooling curves.

notes.heading: The Three States of Matter
notes.body: All matter exists in one of three states: solid, liquid, or gas. The state depends on how strongly the particles are held together, which depends on temperature and pressure. Solids: particles are tightly packed in a regular arrangement, vibrate in fixed positions, strong forces of attraction. Properties: fixed shape, fixed volume, cannot be compressed (particles already touching), high density. Liquids: particles are close together but in a random arrangement, can slide past each other, weaker forces than solids. Properties: no fixed shape (takes shape of container), fixed volume, cannot be compressed, moderate density. Gases: particles are far apart with no arrangement, move rapidly in all directions, very weak forces. Properties: no fixed shape, no fixed volume (fills container), CAN be compressed (large spaces between particles), low density. The particle model explains these properties. Key limitation: the particle model treats particles as tiny solid spheres — it does NOT account for intermolecular forces, particle size variation, or quantum effects. For MYP, this simplified model is sufficient.

illustration.alt: Diagram comparing particle arrangement and motion in solids, liquids, and gases.
illustration.caption: The particle model shows how solids, liquids, and gases differ in packing, arrangement, and movement.

notes.heading: Changes of State
notes.body: Changes of state are PHYSICAL changes — no new substance is made, only the arrangement and energy of particles change. Six changes: Melting (solid → liquid) — particles gain energy, vibrate more, break free from fixed positions. Freezing (liquid → solid) — reverse of melting. Boiling/evaporation (liquid → gas). Condensation (gas → liquid). Sublimation (solid → gas directly, skipping liquid) — e.g., solid CO₂ (dry ice), iodine. Deposition (gas → solid directly) — e.g., frost forming. During melting and boiling, the temperature stays constant even though heating continues — this energy is used to break intermolecular forces (latent heat), NOT to increase kinetic energy. At the melting point, solid and liquid coexist. At the boiling point, liquid and gas coexist. The melting/boiling points are characteristic physical properties used to identify pure substances. Impurities lower the melting point and increase the boiling point (e.g., salt lowers the freezing point of water — why roads are gritted in winter).

illustration.alt: Diagram showing the six changes of state between solid, liquid, and gas.
illustration.caption: Heating drives melting, boiling, and sublimation; cooling drives freezing, condensation, and deposition.

notes.heading: Heating and Cooling Curves
notes.body: A heating curve graphs temperature vs time as a solid is heated to a gas. Key features: (1) Initial slope: solid warms up (kinetic energy increases). (2) First plateau (melting): temperature constant at melting point — energy used to break bonds (latent heat of fusion). Solid and liquid coexist. (3) Rising slope: liquid warms up. (4) Second plateau (boiling): temperature constant at boiling point — energy used to separate particles completely (latent heat of vaporisation). Liquid and gas coexist. (5) Final slope: gas warms up. A cooling curve is the reverse. Important: the melting and boiling plateaus are longer than the warming phases because breaking/forming bonds requires much more energy than simply raising temperature. The specific heat capacity of a substance determines how quickly its temperature rises (water has a high specific heat capacity — it heats up and cools down slowly, which is why coastal climates are moderate).

illustration.alt: Heating curve graph showing temperature over time with melting and boiling plateaus.
illustration.caption: Plateaus represent latent heat: energy breaks intermolecular bonds without changing temperature.

notes.heading: Diffusion
notes.body: Diffusion is the net movement of particles from an area of high concentration to low concentration, resulting from random particle motion. It occurs in liquids and gases (not solids — particles are fixed). Diffusion is faster in gases than liquids because gas particles move faster and have more space between them. Factors affecting diffusion rate: (1) Temperature — higher temperature = particles have more kinetic energy = move faster = faster diffusion. (2) Particle mass — lighter particles diffuse faster than heavier ones at the same temperature (e.g., ammonia (NH₃, Mᵣ=17) diffuses faster than hydrogen chloride (HCl, Mᵣ=36.5)). (3) Concentration gradient — steeper gradient = faster diffusion. Demonstrating diffusion: (1) Potassium manganate(VII) crystal in water — purple colour slowly spreads. (2) Bromine gas in a gas jar — brown colour diffuses upwards. (3) Ammonia + HCl in a glass tube — they diffuse towards each other, and a white ring of NH₄Cl forms closer to the HCl end (because NH₃ is lighter and diffuses faster).

illustration.alt: Diagram showing particles spreading from high concentration to uniform concentration through diffusion.
illustration.caption: Random particle motion produces a net movement from high to low concentration until evenly spread.

notes.heading: Gas Pressure
notes.body: Gas pressure is caused by gas particles colliding with the walls of their container. Each collision exerts a tiny force; billions of collisions per second create measurable pressure. Factors affecting gas pressure: (1) Temperature — increase temperature → particles move faster → collide more often and with more force → pressure increases (at constant volume). (2) Volume — decrease volume (compress) → particles hit walls more frequently → pressure increases (at constant temperature). This is Boyle's Law: pressure × volume = constant (at constant temperature). P₁V₁ = P₂V₂. (3) Number of particles — more particles → more collisions → higher pressure. This is why inflating a balloon increases pressure. Real-world examples: a tyre heats up on a long journey → air inside expands → pressure increases. Aerosol cans warn against heating — the pressure could cause explosion. Deep-sea fish brought to the surface: the reduced pressure causes gases in their body to expand, often fatally (barotrauma). Syringe: pulling the plunger increases volume → decreases pressure → liquid drawn in.

illustration.alt: Diagram showing gas particles colliding with the walls of a container to create pressure.
illustration.caption: Pressure is the total force from billions of particle collisions on the container walls.

notes.heading: Evaporation vs Boiling
notes.body: Evaporation and boiling both convert liquid to gas, but they are different processes. Evaporation: occurs at ANY temperature, only at the SURFACE of the liquid. The fastest-moving particles at the surface have enough energy to escape. This cools the remaining liquid (the average kinetic energy decreases) — why sweating cools you down. Factors increasing evaporation rate: higher temperature, larger surface area, moving air (wind removes vapour), lower humidity. Boiling: occurs at a SPECIFIC temperature (the boiling point), throughout the ENTIRE liquid (bubbles form within). Temperature remains constant during boiling. The boiling point depends on atmospheric pressure — at high altitudes, lower pressure means water boils below 100°C (affects cooking times — food takes longer to cook in the mountains). A liquid boils when its vapour pressure equals the external atmospheric pressure. This is why water boils at a lower temperature at high altitude.

illustration.alt: Comparison diagram showing evaporation at the surface and boiling throughout the liquid.
illustration.caption: Evaporation happens only at the surface at any temperature; boiling occurs throughout at the boiling point.

notes.heading: Limitations of the Particle Model
notes.body: The particle model is a simplified representation with important limitations: (1) It treats all particles as identical solid spheres — real atoms and molecules have different sizes, shapes, and structures. (2) It ignores intermolecular forces — in reality, there are attractions between particles (dipole-dipole, hydrogen bonds, van der Waals forces) that explain why substances have different melting/boiling points. (3) It doesn't account for the space taken up by particles themselves — at very high pressures, particle volume becomes significant (gases deviate from ideal behaviour). (4) It doesn't show that particles are in constant motion even in solids (vibration). Despite these limitations, the particle model successfully explains: why solids/liquids cannot be compressed but gases can, why solids have fixed shapes, why diffusion occurs, how changes of state work, and gas pressure. In later studies, more sophisticated models (kinetic theory of gases, quantum mechanics) address these limitations. For MYP, understanding both the power AND limitations of models is key.

illustration.alt: Diagram contrasting the simplified particle model with real particles of different sizes, shapes, and forces.
illustration.caption: The particle model is useful but oversimplifies real particles and ignores intermolecular forces.

flashcards.definition: Particles tightly packed in regular arrangement, vibrate in fixed positions, strong forces. Fixed shape and volume.
flashcards.example: Ice has a fixed shape and volume — particles are held in a crystal lattice.

flashcards.definition: Particles close together in random arrangement, slide past each other. No fixed shape, fixed volume.
flashcards.example: Water takes the shape of its container but has a fixed volume.

flashcards.definition: Particles far apart, move rapidly in all directions, very weak forces. No fixed shape or volume, compressible.
flashcards.example: Air fills any container completely and can be compressed (e.g., in a bicycle pump).

flashcards.definition: The temperature at which a solid turns to liquid. Temperature stays constant during melting as energy breaks bonds (latent heat).
flashcards.example: Ice melts at 0°C. Pure substances have sharp melting points; impurities lower and broaden the melting range.

flashcards.definition: The temperature at which a liquid turns to gas throughout (not just at surface). Varies with atmospheric pressure.
flashcards.example: Water boils at 100°C at sea level but at ~95°C in Denver (high altitude, lower pressure).

flashcards.definition: Direct change from solid to gas, skipping the liquid phase. Occurs in substances with weak intermolecular forces.
flashcards.example: Solid CO₂ (dry ice) sublimes at −78°C — it produces fog effects without leaving a liquid puddle.

flashcards.definition: Net movement of particles from high to low concentration due to random motion. Faster in gases, faster at higher temperatures.
flashcards.example: Ammonia and HCl diffuse in a tube: NH₃ (lighter) travels faster, white NH₄Cl ring forms closer to HCl end.

flashcards.definition: Energy absorbed or released during a change of state WITHOUT changing temperature. Used to break or form intermolecular bonds.
flashcards.example: During melting, temperature plateaus despite continuous heating — energy goes into breaking the solid structure, not raising temperature.

flashcards.definition: For a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature: pressure × volume = constant. P₁V₁ = P₂V₂.
flashcards.example: Compressing a gas to half its volume doubles the pressure (more frequent particle collisions with walls).

flashcards.definition: Evaporation: surface only, any temperature, causes cooling. Boiling: entire liquid, specific temperature, temperature constant.
flashcards.example: Sweat evaporating cools your skin. Water boiling at 100°C produces bubbles throughout.

flashcards.definition: Energy required to raise 1 kg of a substance by 1°C. Water has a high SHC — it heats/cools slowly.
flashcards.example: Coastal areas have milder climates because the sea absorbs and releases heat slowly.

flashcards.definition: Caused by billions of gas particles colliding with container walls. Increases with temperature, decreases with larger volume.
flashcards.example: A car tyre pressure increases on a hot day — gas particles move faster and hit the walls more forcefully.

questions.stem: Why can gases be compressed but solids cannot?
choices: Gas particles are softer
Gas particles are far apart with empty space between them; solid particles are already touching
Gas particles are smaller
Solids resist all forces
questions.explanation: In gases, particles have large spaces between them — they can be pushed closer together. In solids, particles are already in contact.

questions.stem: During melting, the temperature remains constant even though heating continues. Why?
choices: The thermometer is broken
Energy is being used to break intermolecular forces (latent heat of fusion) rather than increasing kinetic energy
Melting absorbs all the heat
The substance stops absorbing energy
questions.explanation: The plateau in a heating curve represents latent heat — energy goes into overcoming forces between particles, not raising temperature.

questions.stem: Sublimation is the change from:
choices: Solid to liquid
Liquid to gas
Solid directly to gas, skipping liquid
Gas to liquid
questions.explanation: Sublimation bypasses the liquid phase. CO₂ (dry ice) and iodine sublime at room temperature.

questions.stem: Ammonia (NH₃, Mᵣ=17) and HCl (Mᵣ=36.5) diffuse from opposite ends of a tube. Where does the white ring form?
choices: Exactly in the middle
Closer to the HCl end — NH₃ is lighter and diffuses faster
Closer to the NH₃ end — HCl is heavier and faster
At both ends simultaneously
questions.explanation: Lighter particles diffuse faster. NH₃ travels further in the same time, so the white NH₄Cl ring forms nearer to the HCl source.

questions.stem: A sealed syringe of air at 100 kPa and 50 cm³ is compressed to 25 cm³. What is the new pressure? (Assume constant temperature.)
choices: 50 kPa
100 kPa
200 kPa
400 kPa
questions.explanation: Boyle's Law: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂. 100 × 50 = P₂ × 25. P₂ = 200 kPa. Halve the volume → double the pressure.

questions.stem: Why does sweating cool you down?
choices: Sweat is cold when it comes out of glands
The fastest-moving water particles escape (evaporation), lowering the average kinetic energy of remaining liquid — cooling the skin
Sweat absorbs heat from the air
Sweat contains chemicals that lower skin temperature
questions.explanation: Evaporation removes the most energetic particles from the liquid surface. The remaining liquid has lower average kinetic energy → cooler temperature.

questions.stem: Water boils at a lower temperature at high altitude. Why?
choices: Water is purer at high altitude
Atmospheric pressure is lower, so water's vapour pressure equals external pressure at a lower temperature
The air is colder, cooling the water
Gravity is weaker, so water boils faster
questions.explanation: Boiling occurs when vapour pressure = external pressure. At altitude, there's less air above you → lower pressure → boiling occurs below 100°C.

questions.stem: Impurities in a substance typically:
choices: Raise the melting point and lower the boiling point
Lower the melting point and raise the boiling point
Have no effect on melting or boiling
Lower both melting and boiling points
questions.explanation: Impurities disrupt the crystal structure (lower melting point) and make it harder for particles to escape (raise boiling point). E.g., salt on icy roads.

questions.stem: A liquid has a fixed volume but no fixed shape. What does the particle model say about liquid particles?
choices: They are fixed in position
They are close together but can slide past each other — strong enough forces for fixed volume, weak enough to allow flow
They are far apart and move freely
They are arranged in a regular pattern
questions.explanation: Liquid particles are still touching (fixed volume) but can move relative to each other (no fixed shape). Forces are intermediate between solids and gases.

questions.stem: Which process is the reverse of sublimation?
choices: Evaporation
Deposition — gas → solid directly
Condensation
Freezing
questions.explanation: Sublimation = solid → gas. Deposition = gas → solid. Frost forming on a cold surface is deposition of water vapour.

questions.stem: Why does a car tyre pressure increase after a long motorway journey?
choices: Air leaks into the tyre from the road
Friction heats the tyre → air inside gets hotter → particles move faster → more frequent and forceful collisions with tyre walls → higher pressure
The tyre stretches, making more space
The rubber contracts, squeezing the air
questions.explanation: Increased temperature → increased kinetic energy of gas particles → more collisions (frequency and force) → higher pressure at constant volume.

questions.stem: Which statement about the particle model is a LIMITATION?
choices: It explains why solids have fixed shapes
It represents all particles as identical solid spheres and ignores intermolecular forces and particle size
It shows that gases can be compressed
It correctly predicts that liquids flow
questions.explanation: The model assumes all particles are identical spheres with no forces between them (or simple forces). Reality: different shapes, sizes, and complex intermolecular forces.

questions.stem: On a heating curve, which plateau is typically LONGER and why?
choices: Melting — particles need more time to rearrange
Boiling — separating particles completely (liquid → gas) requires much more energy than just loosening them (solid → liquid)
Neither — they are always equal
The first plateau — the solid is coldest
questions.explanation: Latent heat of vaporisation > latent heat of fusion. Completely freeing particles from each other (boiling) requires more energy than just freeing them from fixed positions (melting).

questions.stem: Why does increasing the temperature increase the rate of diffusion?
choices: Particles become smaller at higher temperatures
Particles gain kinetic energy → move faster → spread out more quickly
Temperature creates more particles
The concentration gradient increases
questions.explanation: Higher temperature = more kinetic energy = faster particle movement = particles spread through the available space more rapidly.

questions.stem: A sealed container of gas is heated. What happens to the pressure and why?
choices: Pressure decreases — particles slow down
Pressure stays the same — temperature doesn't affect pressure
Pressure increases — particles move faster and hit the walls more often and with more force
Pressure fluctuates randomly
questions.explanation: At constant volume, increasing temperature → particles gain kinetic energy → collide more frequently and forcefully with walls → pressure rises.

questions.stem: Water vapour in the air forms droplets on the outside of a cold glass. What is this change of state called?
choices: Evaporation
Condensation — gas to liquid
Freezing
Sublimation
questions.explanation: Condensation is the change from gas to liquid. Water vapour loses energy on contact with the cold surface and turns back into liquid droplets.

questions.stem: Why is salt spread on roads in icy weather?
choices: Salt raises the freezing point of water
Salt lowers the freezing point of water, so ice melts even below 0°C
Salt absorbs the ice like a sponge
Salt warms up the road surface
questions.explanation: Dissolved salt is an impurity: it lowers water's freezing point, so ice turns back into liquid even when the air is a few degrees below 0°C.

questions.stem: Why is diffusion much faster in gases than in liquids?
choices: Gas particles are smaller than liquid particles
Gas particles move faster and have more space to travel through
Liquids cannot diffuse at all
Gas particles attract each other more strongly
questions.explanation: Gas particles move rapidly with large gaps between them, so they spread through the available space quickly. Liquid particles are close together and move more slowly, so diffusion is slower.

questions.stem: On a cooling curve, the temperature stays constant while a liquid freezes, even though the substance keeps losing heat to the surroundings. Why?
choices: The substance stops losing energy during freezing
Energy is released as particles form intermolecular bonds — this balances the heat lost, so the temperature does not fall
The thermometer cannot measure below room temperature
Freezing gives the particles extra kinetic energy
questions.explanation: Freezing is the reverse of melting: as bonds form between particles, latent heat is given out. This released energy replaces the heat lost to the surroundings, holding the temperature at the freezing point until all the liquid has solidified.

questions.stem: A sealed syringe contains gas at 150 kPa and 40 cm³. The gas slowly expands to 60 cm³ at constant temperature. What is the new pressure?
choices: 90 kPa
100 kPa
150 kPa
225 kPa
questions.explanation: Boyle's Law: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂. 150 × 40 = P₂ × 60, so P₂ = 6000 ÷ 60 = 100 kPa. Larger volume → particles hit the walls less often → lower pressure.

questions.stem: A damp cloth wrapped around a water bottle helps keep the water cool on a hot day. Why?
choices: The cloth blocks all heat from reaching the bottle
Water evaporating from the cloth removes the fastest-moving particles, lowering the average kinetic energy of the water left behind
The cloth releases cold air as it dries
Evaporation adds energy to the bottle
questions.explanation: Evaporation is a cooling process: the most energetic particles escape from the damp cloth's surface, so the water left in the cloth has a lower average kinetic energy. Heat then flows from the bottle into the cooler cloth.

questions.stem: Aerosol cans carry a warning: 'do not expose to temperatures above 50°C'. In terms of particles, what is the risk?
choices: The gas particles expand and split the can open
Heating makes the gas particles move faster, so they collide with the can walls more often and more forcefully — the pressure may rise until the can bursts
The metal of the can melts at 50°C
Heat turns the gas into a liquid, which overflows
questions.explanation: At constant volume, raising the temperature increases the kinetic energy of the gas particles. More frequent and more forceful collisions with the walls mean higher pressure, which can exceed what the can is built to withstand.

questions.stem: Which statement about evaporation is correct?
choices: It happens only at the boiling point
It happens at any temperature, but only at the liquid's surface
It produces bubbles throughout the liquid
It occurs only in pure water
questions.explanation: Evaporation occurs at all temperatures because the fastest particles at the surface can always escape. Bubbles forming throughout the liquid describe boiling, which happens only at the boiling point.

questions.stem: A pan of water is heated until bubbles of gas form throughout the liquid and rise to the surface. The temperature stays at 100°C. This process is best described as:
choices: Evaporation, because gas is leaving the liquid
Boiling, because it happens throughout the liquid at a constant, specific temperature
Condensation, because gas is moving upwards
Sublimation, because no temperature change occurs
questions.explanation: Boiling takes place throughout the whole liquid — bubbles form within it — at one specific temperature. Evaporation happens only at the surface and at any temperature.

questions.stem: At the same temperature, which of these gases diffuses fastest?
choices: Carbon dioxide (CO₂, Mᵣ=44)
Oxygen (O₂, Mᵣ=32)
Ammonia (NH₃, Mᵣ=17)
Chlorine (Cl₂, Mᵣ=71)
questions.explanation: At a given temperature, lighter particles move faster on average, so the gas with the lowest Mᵣ diffuses fastest. NH₃ (Mᵣ=17) is the lightest gas listed.

questions.stem: A pressure cooker cooks food faster than an open pan. Why?
choices: It traps heat, so less energy is wasted
The increased pressure raises water's boiling point above 100°C, so the food cooks at a higher temperature
Steam conducts electricity better than liquid water
The high pressure physically breaks the food apart
questions.explanation: Boiling starts when vapour pressure equals external pressure. Raising the pressure inside the cooker pushes the boiling point above 100°C, and food cooks faster at the higher temperature — the reverse of the high-altitude effect.

questions.stem: A weather balloon is only partly filled with helium at launch. As it rises, the balloon swells and may eventually burst. Why?
choices: The helium heats up and its particles multiply
External air pressure falls with altitude, so the higher pressure inside the balloon pushes the walls outwards until the rubber fails
UV radiation weakens the helium particles
Gravity pulls harder on the balloon at high altitude
questions.explanation: Atmospheric pressure decreases with altitude. With less external pressure balancing it, the internal gas pressure expands the balloon; the volume grows until the material can stretch no further and the balloon bursts.

questions.stem: Steam at 100°C causes much worse burns than boiling water at 100°C. Why?
choices: Steam particles are larger than water particles
Steam releases a large amount of latent heat when it condenses on the skin, before the resulting water even begins to cool
Steam is at a higher temperature than boiling water
Boiling water evaporates before it touches the skin
questions.explanation: Condensing steam gives out the latent heat of vaporisation — the same large quantity of energy that makes boiling the longer plateau on a heating curve. The skin absorbs this energy first, then more heat as the condensed water cools from 100°C.
